name: Russian Blue
lede: Russian Blue is a pale, greyed blue, a name the books record but barely explain.

sections.title: A pale blue with a country on it
sections.body:
Paterson's dictionary defines Russian blue in a single phrase: a light blue [1]. It appears again in his index of blues, with no further note on where the name came from [2][3]. The books in our collection give no dated origin, no pigment and no dye for it, so the geography is best read as a trade or fashion label rather than a recipe [1][2].

The swatch here is a cool, grey-tinted blue, close to [[light-blue]] and to [[powder-blue]] and [[sky-blue]] in lightness [4]. The name is also borne by a grey-blue cat breed, but the books do not discuss that link [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our archive of 23,781 paintings, 332 hold this color at 5% of the canvas or more, as photographed [4]. Printed use of the phrase *russian blue* climbed late: it reached its peak in 1997, far above its showing in the 1800s [5].

origin.source: Paterson, A Dictionary of Colour, p. 350

openers: Russian blue is defined in one phrase, a light blue, and its origin is undocumented in the books.
Printed use of 'Russian blue' peaked in 1997, long after the color word first appeared.
